name: Jamal Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Jamal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Weekdays I do takeaway on a 125 scooter in the suburbs on the north side, five till eleven, mostly pizza and curry to housing estates. Saturdays and Sundays I take parcel blocks on a flex app, where you pick up from a big warehouse at six in the morning and deliver from your own car until you're done. I rent a room in a shared house near the train line and send my mum a bit each month. I've been doing this about a year and a half, and I'm still learning which estates have gates that need codes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out most, and what do you actually like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The weekend parcel blocks wear me out, because the app guesses you'll finish in four hours and it always takes me five and a half. Nobody pays the extra ninety minutes. What I like is the scooter at night with the streets empty. And regulars: there's a nurse on Fenwick Road who orders the same curry every Thursday after her shift and always says thanks like she means it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, I never thought it was going to change much for me. At work I'd say the same. I don't really post about this kind of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's mostly fine. My hours and pay stay roughly the same, which isn't great, but it's known. The bit that bothers me is simple. I'm working seven days a week to have a decent month, and that's not AI's fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep both jobs going. I'd try to get my savings from about two months up to four, by cutting out the weekend nights out. I'd maybe use the AI chat on my phone to tidy up my CV, which I've done once before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish, but tired. Seven days a week wears you down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if you dropped the weekend parcel blocks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lose about a third of my money. Rent would be fine but I couldn't send anything to my mum. So I don't drop them, even when I'm wrecked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you talk to about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Andre, who drives city buses. He's always telling me to do my bus licence, because there's a union and a pension. I keep saying next year.

say: I'd say I never expected AI to **change much** for me.
I **don't post** about this kind of thing.
think: My pay stays roughly the same, which is **known**, if not great.
My real issue is working **seven days** to have a decent month.
do: Keep the **takeaway evenings** and weekend parcel blocks going.
Grow savings from **two months to four** by skipping weekend nights out.
feel: Calm-ish but **tired** from working **seven days** a week.
S0.quote: I'm working seven days a week to have a decent month, and that's not AI's fault.
fieldNote: He relies on **two gig jobs** to cover rent and money for his mum.
His cousin's **bus licence** idea keeps coming up, but he keeps delaying.
He isn't losing income, but the **seven-day week** is a steady strain.

steps.text: Keep scooter takeaway evenings and weekend parcel blocks
Skip weekend nights out to grow savings to four months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should learn to work with it and stop panicking. I'd say it at work and maybe to my mum, who worries. I wouldn't go online about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job's mostly fine for a while, because someone still has to carry the food to the door. The parcel app might get stricter, with software deciding who gets blocks. If more office people start doing flex blocks at weekends, I'd lose some.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going but watch the parcel blocks. If they started drying up, I'd ask Andre how he got into the bus company, because he's done it and it worked. I'd use the AI chat a bit more, maybe to work out my real hourly pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not scared, just watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know the blocks were drying up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When I open the parcel app on Friday night and there's nothing for Saturday, that's my signal. It's happened twice this autumn already. If it's every week, that's my signal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't self-driving buses be a risk too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, yeah. Andre says passengers want a driver, especially at night. I'd want to see buses with no driver actually running before I worried about that.

say: I'd say people should **learn to work** with AI and stop panicking.
I'd tell my mum, who **worries**, not to fret.
think: Someone still has to **carry food** to the door, so I'm fine for a while.
More **office workers** doing weekend blocks could cut my parcel shifts.
do: Watch whether **parcel blocks** dry up on Friday nights.
Ask Andre how he got into the **bus company** if they do.
Use an **AI chat** to work out his real hourly pay.
S1.quote: When I open the parcel app on Friday night and there's nothing for Saturday, that's my signal.
fieldNote: He has a clear **signal** to act, empty Friday blocks, which fits his wait-for-proof style.
He trusts his cousin's **bus job** because he's seen it work.
He judges his own job mostly **safe** here, with some risk to weekend income.

steps.text: Check each Friday whether weekend parcel blocks are appearing
Use the phone AI chat to work out his real hourly pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening too fast and nobody's ready. I'd say the government needs to slow it down or help people through it, one or the other. At work, I'd say it plainly: we're all in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I lose both jobs by 2031, and so does Andre, because a robot bus is easier than a robot delivery. For three years I'd still be riding the scooter, but the apps would be run by AI and I'd have no one to complain to. At thirty-two I'd have nothing on my CV but driving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop thinking about the bus licence, because buses go too. I'd look at hospital porter jobs, because there's a big hospital near me and it's people work. I'd cut my spending hard, stop the car insurance by selling the car, and do scooter only.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, really. Like the ground's tilting and you can't find anything to hold on to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum I might not be able to send money for a while, but I'm looking. She'd tell me to come home, and I don't want to. I'd say give me six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a hospital porter rather than something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen the porters on my deliveries, pushing beds, chatting to patients. Someone has to be there when a person's frightened. I don't know if robots will do that too, but I think people would want a person.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and nobody's ready for it.
I'd tell workmates plainly that we're **all in trouble**, buses included.
think: I lose **both jobs** by 2031, and Andre's bus job goes too.
At **thirty-two** I'd have nothing on my CV but driving.
do: Drop the **bus licence** plan and apply for **hospital porter** jobs.
Sell the **car** and do scooter deliveries only.
feel: **Scared**, like the ground is tilting with nothing to hold.
S2.quote: I'd tell my mum I might not be able to send money for a while, but I'm looking.
fieldNote: The fast picture kills his **fallback plan**, his cousin's bus route.
He turns to **people work** at the local hospital as the next proven path.
He worries about letting down his **mum**, whom he supports.

steps.text: Apply for porter jobs at the hospital near his house
Sell the car and drop the weekend parcel blocks
Cut nights out and stop sending extra money to his mum

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's some time, so use it. I'd tell the younger lads on the scooters to start thinking now. I'd still say the government should help people move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is enough time to do one proper change, but not two. I'd have to pick right the first time. Robots by 2034 means I'm thirty-five, and I'd want to be settled in something by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what happens to buses and hospitals in the first two years. If hospitals are still hiring porters by 2028, I'd apply there and keep the scooter evenings. I'd save hard, aiming for six months of rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can live with. More like before an exam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if you pick wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm thirty-five and starting again, which isn't the end of the world. Plenty of people do it. I'd just rather not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your cousin Andre say about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Andre would say stick with buses, people want a driver. He's been right before. I'd listen, but I'd watch for buses with no drivers in other cities.

say: I'd say there's **some time**, so people should use it.
I'd tell younger riders to **start thinking** now, and want government help to move.
think: Five years is enough for **one change**, not two, so I must pick right.
I want to be **settled** in something by thirty-five.
do: Watch **buses and hospitals** for the first two years.
Apply to be a **hospital porter** by 2028 if they're hiring.
Save hard toward **six months** of rent.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time to do one proper change, but not two.
fieldNote: He frames the extra time as **one chance** to switch, which worries him.
His **cousin's advice** still pulls him toward buses despite the risk.
He still expects driving to **end**, so the mood stays anxious.

steps.text: Watch hiring at buses and the hospital for two years
Apply for a hospital porter job by 2028
Save toward six months of rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a lot of time, and people should use it calmly. I'd say it at work. I'd probably tell my mum it's nothing to worry about yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private, ten years feels like I can actually think. I'd do the bus licence like Andre says, drive buses for a few years, and look again before 2039. I'd be thirty-nine then, which isn't old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the scooter evenings for a year or two, then take the bus licence course when the bus company is paying for it. I'd drop the weekend parcel blocks once the bus job starts. I'd keep saving steadily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A little uneasy, but it feels far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the bus now and not the hospital?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with ten years, the bus pays better and has a pension, and Andre can get me in. If I see robot buses coming, I'd still have time to move to the hospital.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss about the scooter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The empty streets at night, and the nurse on Fenwick Road with her Thursday curry. A bus is different. On a bus you see hundreds of people, but you don't know any of them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it kills my plan and Andre's job in one go. What would help is somebody telling us clearly which jobs will still need people in five years, and paying for the training. I'd do it, I just need to see it's real first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my mum. A lot of drivers send money home, and if delivery jobs go, people back home feel it too. That's the bit nobody counts.

headlineQuote: A lot of drivers send money home, and if delivery jobs go, people back home feel it too.
portrait: Jamal is a **27-year-old** who delivers takeaway by scooter on weeknights and parcels on weekends.
He rents a room, works **seven days**, and sends money to his mum.
He's **pragmatic**, waits for proof, and trusts his cousin Andre's bus career.
He's **uneasy** in the slow pictures and alarmed when AGI arrives in 2028.
With ten years he'd take the **bus licence**, keeping the hospital as a back-up.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it wipes out both his job and his cousin's bus route.
whatWouldHelp: Clear word on **which jobs** will still need people, and **paid training**.
